text: Every restore so far has assumed the target server matches the source server's folder structure. In practice, refreshing a staging environment or rebuilding after a total server loss both mean restoring onto a server whose drive layout doesn't match at all.

A backup stores the exact physical file paths the database used when it was backed up. If the target server doesn't have that same drive or folder, a plain restore fails immediately, because SQL Server tries to recreate the files at those exact paths.

MOVE tells SQL Server to use the backup's data but write the files somewhere else. Each file needs its own MOVE, referenced by its logical name — which RESTORE FILELISTONLY reveals. You can rename the database itself in the same statement.

A restored database keeps its database-level users, but SQL Server logins are server-level objects stored separately. Without a matching login on the new server, that user becomes orphaned — it exists but can't authenticate. sp_change_users_login finds and fixes it.

This is the same login-versus-user distinction from T-SQL for DBAs, showing back up in a restore context. Next up: tail-log backups, the step that captures transactions the moment before a restore begins.
